decks.title: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers — Part 1: Forming the Government
goals: Explain how the President appoints the Prime Minister, including in a hung House
Describe how the Council of Ministers is formed, its tenure and the limit on its size
Name the three ranks of ministers and their roles
Distinguish the Council of Ministers from the Cabinet

slides.heading: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers
slides.body_md: Part 1 — who becomes **Prime Minister**, how the **ministry** is formed, how long it lasts and how **big** it can be.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: appointing the Prime Minister, forming the Council of Ministers, its tenure and size, the three ranks of ministers, and the difference between the Council and the Cabinet
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: In the last chapter we met the President, the head of the State. But the day to day work of the Union government is done by the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers. In this part we see how the Prime Minister is chosen, how ministers are appointed, how long the ministry stays in office, and how the Cabinet differs from the larger Council.

slides.heading: Forming the government

nodes.label: General election to the Lok Sabha
Clear majority? President invites its leader
No majority? President judges who can win a confidence vote
Prime Minister appointed and sworn in
Other ministers appointed on the Prime Minister's advice

visual.alt: Flow of forming the government: after a Lok Sabha election the President invites the leader of the majority, or in a hung House judges who can win a confidence vote; the Prime Minister is sworn in and the other ministers are appointed on the Prime Minister's advice
visual.caption: How a government is formed.

slides.narration: After a general election to the Lok Sabha, the President invites the leader of the party or alliance that has a majority, and appoints that leader as Prime Minister. The other ministers are then appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. Everything depends on support in the Lok Sabha, the directly elected House.

slides.heading: When the President has a choice
slides.body_md: If one party or a pre-poll alliance has a **clear majority**, its leader **must** be invited. In a **hung House**, the President uses **discretion**.
bullets: Invite the leader most likely to **win a vote of confidence**.
The new Prime Minister may be asked to **prove the majority** on the floor within a set time.
slides.narration: Usually the President has no real choice: the leader of the majority must be invited. Discretion arises only when no party or alliance has a majority. Then the President judges which leader is most likely to win a vote of confidence in the Lok Sabha, and may ask that leader to prove it on the floor of the House within a set time.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a hung House
slides.body_md: An imagined result: Party P 248, Party Q 182, Party R 61, others 52 in a House of 543.
bullets: Step 1 — Majority mark: half of 543, plus one, is 272.
Step 2 — No party reaches it alone.
Step 3 — P and R together: 248 plus 61 is 309, above 272.
Step 4 — The President invites the P–R alliance leader, who proves the majority in a confidence vote.

slides.narration: Let us work through an imagined result. The majority mark in a House of 543 is 272. Party P, with 248 seats, falls short. But P and R together have 309 seats, more than enough. So the President would invite the leader of their alliance, who would then win a vote of confidence. Notice that being the second largest party gives Q no claim.

slides.heading: Quick check: tenure
slides.body_md: How long does the Council of Ministers stay in office in practice?
slides.narration: The phrase in the Constitution is during the pleasure of the President. But think about whose support really keeps a government alive.

slides.heading: Four rules about the ministry

rows: President appoints the Prime Minister; other ministers on the Prime Minister's advice
Not more than 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha strength, including the Prime Minister (81 for 543)
During the pleasure of the President: in practice while the Lok Sabha supports the ministry
Must enter either House within 6 months

visual.alt: Table of four constitutional rules on the ministry: appointment by the President, size limited to 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha, tenure during the pleasure of the President, and the six-month rule for non-members

slides.narration: Four rules in Article seventy-five shape the ministry. The President appoints the Prime Minister and, on the Prime Minister's advice, the other ministers. The total cannot be more than fifteen per cent of the Lok Sabha. Ministers hold office during the President's pleasure, which in practice means as long as the Lok Sabha supports them. And a minister who is not in Parliament must enter it within six months.

slides.heading: Tenure: no fixed term
bullets: Ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President**.
The President acts on the **Prime Minister's advice**, so a minister stays as long as the Prime Minister wants.
The **whole ministry** stays as long as it keeps the **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.
A **non-member** can be a minister for up to **six months**.
slides.narration: The ministry has no fixed term. On paper it serves at the pleasure of the President, but the President acts on ministerial advice, so the real test is the Lok Sabha. A government that loses the support of the Lok Sabha must go. A person who is not a member of either House may become a minister, but must enter Parliament within six months.

slides.heading: How big can the ministry be?
slides.body_md: The **91st Amendment (2003)** limits the ministry, **including the Prime Minister**, to **15 per cent** of the Lok Sabha strength.

slides.narration: Before two thousand and three, ministries were sometimes very large, partly to reward supporters. The ninety-first amendment fixed a ceiling: the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, cannot be more than fifteen per cent of the strength of the Lok Sabha. With 543 members, that is at most 81 ministers.

slides.heading: Quick check: the size limit
slides.body_md: Which amendment added the 15 per cent ceiling?
slides.narration: The same amendment of two thousand and three also tightened the Anti-Defection Law. Recall its number.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: is this ministry allowed?
slides.body_md: An imagined new government wants 90 ministers, including the Prime Minister, in a Lok Sabha of 543.
bullets: Step 1 — 15 per cent of 543 is 81.45.
Step 2 — Round down: at most 81 ministers.
Step 3 — 90 is more than the limit, so 9 ministers must be dropped.
Step 4 — In the exam, state the rule, the calculation and the amendment.

visual.alt: Table of the worked example: Lok Sabha 543, 15 per cent is 81.45, the largest ministry allowed is 81, the proposed ministry of 90 exceeds it by 9

slides.narration: Here is how to check the size of a ministry. Fifteen per cent of 543 is eighty one point four five. A minister is a whole person, so the most allowed is 81. A plan for ninety ministers is nine too many. In an answer, state the rule, show the working, and name the ninety-first amendment.

slides.heading: Three ranks of ministers

slides.narration: The Council of Ministers has three ranks. Cabinet Ministers head the most important ministries and form the inner core. Ministers of State either help a Cabinet Minister or hold independent charge of a smaller ministry. Deputy Ministers assist senior ministers and have no charge of their own. At the top is the Prime Minister, who leads them all.

slides.heading: What each rank does

rows: Helps a Cabinet Minister or holds independent charge
Assists senior ministers; no charge of his own

visual.alt: Table of the three ranks of ministers: Cabinet Ministers head important ministries and attend the Cabinet; Ministers of State help or hold independent charge and attend only when invited; Deputy Ministers assist and do not attend

slides.narration: This table sums up the ranks. Only Cabinet Ministers are members of the Cabinet and attend its meetings as of right. A Minister of State attends only when a matter of his or her ministry is discussed. Deputy Ministers do not attend Cabinet meetings at all. Remember the phrase independent charge: it means a Minister of State runs a ministry without a Cabinet Minister above.

slides.heading: Quick check: the three ranks
slides.body_md: Which three ranks make up the Council of Ministers?
slides.narration: Look for the option in which every name is a kind of minister.

slides.heading: Council of Ministers and Cabinet
slides.body_md: The **Cabinet** is the **inner group** of senior ministers inside the larger **Council of Ministers**.
bullets: The Council is large and **rarely meets** as one body.
The Cabinet meets **regularly** and takes the main decisions.
The Constitution speaks of the **Council**; the word Cabinet appears once, in the emergency provision.
slides.narration: People often use the words Cabinet and Council of Ministers as if they meant the same thing. They do not. The Council is the whole ministry of all three ranks, too large to discuss policy in detail. The Cabinet is the small inner group of senior ministers that meets regularly and takes the real decisions, which the Council then carries out.

slides.heading: Comparing the two bodies

rows: Meets regularly under the Prime Minister
Must advise a national emergency in writing

visual.alt: Table comparing the Council of Ministers and the Cabinet by members, size, meetings, role and part in a national emergency

slides.narration: Compare them point by point. The Council has all three ranks; the Cabinet only Cabinet Ministers. The Council is large; the Cabinet small. The Council rarely meets as one body; the Cabinet meets regularly under the Prime Minister. The Cabinet decides policy; the Council carries it out. And a national emergency needs the written advice of the Cabinet.

slides.heading: Quick check: a Rajya Sabha Prime Minister?
slides.body_md: True or false: a member of the Rajya Sabha can become Prime Minister.
slides.narration: Ask what the Constitution requires: membership of a particular House, or the support of a particular House?

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: President appoints the **Prime Minister**: the majority leader, or by **discretion** in a hung House.
Other ministers appointed **on the Prime Minister's advice**; non-members must enter Parliament within **six months**.
No fixed term: in office while the **Lok Sabha** supports it; size at most **15 per cent** (81).
Three ranks; the **Cabinet** is the decision-making core of the **Council**.

slides.narration: To sum up. The President appoints the leader who can command a majority in the Lok Sabha as Prime Minister, and the other ministers on that leader's advice. The ministry has no fixed term and lasts while the Lok Sabha supports it, and it cannot be more than fifteen per cent of the House. Of its three ranks, the Cabinet Ministers form the Cabinet, the real centre of decisions.

slides.heading: Exam tips for Part 1
bullets: The President **appoints** the Prime Minister but has **discretion** only in a hung House.
Write "**15 per cent of the Lok Sabha, including the Prime Minister**" and name the **91st Amendment (2003)**.
Keep **Council of Ministers** and **Cabinet** apart; give size, members and role.
In 3 + 3 + 4 questions, write one clear point per mark and show any calculation.
slides.narration: Common slips to avoid. The President's discretion applies only when no one has a majority. The size limit includes the Prime Minister and comes from the ninety-first amendment. Never use Cabinet and Council of Ministers as if they were the same. In long questions, give one clear point for each mark and show your working in any calculation.

decks.title: The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers — Part 2: Cabinet, Responsibility and the Prime Minister
goals: Explain the policy-making, administrative, legislative, financial and emergency functions of the Cabinet
Distinguish collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha from individual responsibility to the President
Explain why the Prime Minister is the real head of the executive
Describe the powers of the Prime Minister in relation to the Cabinet, the President and Parliament

slides.heading: How the Union government is steered
slides.body_md: Part 2 — what the **Cabinet** does, how ministers are held **responsible**, and why the **Prime Minister** is the key figure.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: functions of the Cabinet, collective and individual responsibility, and the position and powers of the Prime Minister
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: Now that we know who the ministers are, we look at what they do. We study the five functions of the Cabinet, the two kinds of responsibility that keep ministers answerable, and finally the position and powers of the Prime Minister, the real head of the Union executive.

slides.heading: Five functions of the Cabinet

rows: Decides which ministry builds a bridge
Approves a wetlands bill for Parliament
Prepares the budget and tax proposals
Approves proposals for the Finance Minister
Advises a national emergency in writing

visual.alt: Table of the five functions of the Cabinet with what each involves and an imagined example: policy making, administrative coordination, legislative, financial and emergency

slides.narration: The Cabinet has five main functions. It makes policy. It runs the administration by coordinating ministries. It decides which bills to bring before Parliament. It prepares the budget and tax proposals. And it advises the President before a national emergency. The examples in the table are imagined, but each shows one function at work.

slides.heading: Policy, administration and law-making
bullets: **Policy making:** decides domestic and foreign policy.
**Administrative:** coordinates ministries, settles disputes, supervises how policies are carried out.
**Legislative:** most bills are government bills; ministers pilot them through Parliament.
slides.narration: The Cabinet decides what the government will do, from farm support to foreign relations. It also makes sure ministries work together: if two ministries disagree, the Cabinet or the Prime Minister settles the matter. And because most laws begin as government bills, the Cabinet decides which bills go to Parliament and its ministers guide them through.

slides.heading: Quick check: a tax by order?
slides.body_md: True or false: the Cabinet can impose a tax by its own order.
slides.narration: Remember the rule that no tax can be collected except by the authority of law.

slides.heading: The emergency safeguard
slides.body_md: Since the **44th Amendment (1978)**, a national emergency needs the **written decision of the Cabinet**.

nodes.label: Approval by both Houses within one month

visual.alt: Flow of a national emergency after the 44th Amendment: Cabinet decision, written recommendation to the President, proclamation, and approval by both Houses within one month
visual.caption: Article 352(3), added by the 44th Amendment (1978).

slides.narration: The Cabinet's financial role is to prepare the budget, which Parliament must approve. Its emergency role became stricter in nineteen seventy eight. The forty fourth amendment says the President can proclaim a national emergency only after the Union Cabinet recommends it in writing. This means the Prime Minister alone cannot advise an emergency; the whole Cabinet must decide.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the function
slides.body_md: Classify four items from an imagined Cabinet meeting.
bullets: A wetlands bill approved for Parliament → **legislative**.
A dispute between two ministries over a dam settled → **administrative** (coordination).
Tax proposals approved for the Finance Minister → **financial**.
A new export policy adopted → **policy making**.

visual.alt: Table classifying four imagined Cabinet decisions: a wetlands bill is legislative, settling a dam dispute is administrative, tax proposals are financial, an export policy is policy making

slides.narration: Practise naming the function. A bill for Parliament shows the legislative function. Settling a dispute between ministries is administrative coordination. Approving tax proposals is financial. Choosing a new export policy is policy making. In the exam, name the function and point to the words in the situation that show it.

slides.heading: Collective responsibility
slides.body_md: Article **75(3)**: the Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible** to the **Lok Sabha**.

visual.alt: Flow of collective responsibility: the Cabinet decides together, every minister defends the decision, and if the Lok Sabha withdraws confidence the whole Council of Ministers resigns
visual.caption: Article 75(3): they stand or fall together.

slides.narration: Collective responsibility means the ministers stand or fall together. Every decision of the Cabinet is the decision of all ministers, and each must defend it in public. A minister who cannot do so should resign. If the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion or rejects the budget, the whole Council of Ministers must resign, not just one minister.

slides.heading: Quick check: to which House?
slides.body_md: To which body is the Council of Ministers collectively responsible?
slides.narration: Only one House can bring down the government. Which one?

slides.heading: Two kinds of responsibility

rows: The President, on the Prime Minister's advice
The work of one minister's department
That minister alone may be removed
Article 75(2): office during the President's pleasure

visual.alt: Table comparing collective responsibility (to the Lok Sabha, for all decisions, whole ministry resigns, Article 75(3)) with individual responsibility (to the President on the Prime Minister's advice, for one department, only that minister removed, Article 75(2))

slides.narration: Compare the two kinds. Collective responsibility is to the Lok Sabha, covers every decision, and if it fails the whole ministry goes. Individual responsibility is to the President, acting on the Prime Minister's advice, covers one minister's department, and if it fails only that minister is removed. Both keep ministers answerable.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which principle applies?
slides.body_md: Two imagined situations in the same government.
bullets: A minister disagrees with a Cabinet decision and wants to attack it in public → **collective**: support it or resign.
Another minister's department fails badly → **individual**: that minister may be asked to resign.
The government continues in the second case; in the first, the minister leaves or falls in line.

rows: Defend it in public or resign

visual.alt: Table of two imagined situations: a minister who disagrees with a Cabinet decision must defend it or resign under collective responsibility; a minister whose department fails may be removed under individual responsibility

slides.narration: Here are two situations. A minister who dislikes a Cabinet decision may argue inside the Cabinet, but once it is taken he must defend it or resign: that is collective responsibility. A minister whose department fails may be asked to quit while the government carries on: that is individual responsibility. Always say which principle you are applying.

slides.narration: The Prime Minister is linked to every part of the system. With the Council of Ministers, the Prime Minister chooses ministers and presides. With the President, the Prime Minister is the link and must communicate decisions. In the Lok Sabha, the Prime Minister leads the majority. And for the nation, the Prime Minister is the chief spokesperson and the crisis manager.

slides.heading: Powers over the ministry
bullets: Advises the President on **appointing and dismissing** ministers.
**Allocates and changes portfolios**.
**Presides over the Cabinet** and **coordinates** all ministries.
If the Prime Minister **resigns or dies**, the **whole Council ends**.
slides.narration: Over the ministry, the Prime Minister's powers are wide. The Prime Minister picks the ministers, gives them their portfolios, and can have any of them removed. The Prime Minister presides over the Cabinet and coordinates the work of all departments. And because the Council exists around the Prime Minister, it comes to an end if the Prime Minister resigns or dies.

But under Article seventy four, the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers, headed by the Prime Minister. So the President is the nominal executive and the Prime Minister the real one, answerable to the Lok Sabha.

sections.heading: 1. Appointing the Prime Minister
sections.body_md:
- **Article 75(1):** the **President** appoints the Prime Minister.
- Normally the leader of the **party or pre-poll alliance with a majority** in the **Lok Sabha** must be invited.
- In a **hung House**, the President uses **discretion**: invites the leader most likely to **win a vote of confidence**, who may be asked to prove the majority within a time.
- The Prime Minister may be from either House, but the government depends on the **Lok Sabha**.

sections.heading: 2. Forming the ministry: tenure and size
sections.body_md:
- Other ministers are appointed by the President **on the Prime Minister's advice**; the President administers the oaths of **office and secrecy**.
- **Tenure:** ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President** (Article 75(2)); in practice the ministry lasts while the **Lok Sabha** supports it, and a minister while the **Prime Minister** wants.
- **Non-member:** must become a member of either House within **6 months** (Article 75(5)).
- **Size:** the total, **including the Prime Minister**, may not exceed **15 per cent** of the Lok Sabha strength (**91st Amendment, 2003**): at most **81** with 543 members.

sections.heading: 3. Three ranks; Council and Cabinet
sections.body_md:
- **Cabinet Ministers:** head important ministries; members of the Cabinet.
- **Ministers of State:** help a Cabinet Minister or hold **independent charge**; attend the Cabinet only **when invited**.
- **Deputy Ministers:** assist senior ministers; no charge of their own.
- The **Council** is large and rarely meets as one body; the **Cabinet** is small, meets regularly and takes the **main decisions**.

sections.heading: 4. Functions of the Cabinet
sections.body_md:
- **Policy making:** domestic and foreign policy.
- **Administrative:** coordinates ministries, settles disputes, supervises implementation.
- **Legislative:** decides government bills; ministers pilot them; advises on summoning and proroguing Parliament.
- **Financial:** prepares the budget and tax proposals presented by the Finance Minister; Parliament must approve them.
- **Emergency:** a national emergency only on the **written decision of the Union Cabinet** (Article 352(3), **44th Amendment, 1978**).

sections.heading: 5. Collective and individual responsibility
sections.body_md:
- **Collective (Article 75(3)):** the Council is responsible to the **Lok Sabha**; ministers **stand or fall together**; a minister who cannot defend a decision should resign; a successful **no-confidence motion** or defeat on the budget removes the **whole ministry**.
- **Individual:** each minister answers for his **department**; holds office during the President's pleasure, so the **Prime Minister** can have him removed without the government falling.
- The **Rajya Sabha** can question ministers but cannot remove the government.

sections.heading: 6. Position and powers of the Prime Minister
sections.body_md:
- **Real executive:** the President acts on the advice of the Council headed by the Prime Minister (**Article 74**); the **42nd Amendment (1976)** made advice binding, the **44th (1978)** allows one reconsideration.
- **Over the ministry:** appoints and removes ministers (through the President), allocates portfolios, presides over the Cabinet, coordinates; the Council ends if the Prime Minister resigns or dies.
- **With the President:** the link; must communicate decisions on administration and legislation (**Article 78**); advises on appointments and dissolution.
- **In Parliament and the nation:** leader of the majority, chief spokesperson, represents the country abroad, crisis manager.
- Strength varies: greater with a **single-party majority**, more limited in a **coalition**.

questions.stem_md: Under the Constitution, which authority formally appoints the Prime Minister of India?

options.text_md: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The President
The Chief Justice of India
The Vice-President

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The President. Article 75 says the Prime Minister is appointed by the President. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, the Chief Justice heads the judiciary, and the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha; none of them appoints the Prime Minister.

questions.stem_md: On whose advice does the President appoint the other members of the Union Council of Ministers?

options.text_md: The Chief Election Commissioner
The Rajya Sabha
The Governors of the States
The Prime Minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Prime Minister. Ministers other than the Prime Minister are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister. The Election Commission, the Rajya Sabha and the Governors have no say in choosing Union ministers.

questions.stem_md: The bar picture shows the seats won by parties in an imagined Lok Sabha of 543 members. No single party has crossed the majority mark. Party P and Party R announce an alliance with a common leader. Whom is the President most likely to invite first to form the government?

options.text_md: The leader of the P–R alliance, because together they have a majority
The leader of Party Q, because it is the second-largest party
The member with the longest service in the House
Nobody: the House must be dissolved at once

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The leader of the P–R alliance, because together they have a majority. Together P and R hold 309 seats, more than the 272 needed, so the alliance leader is the person most likely to command the confidence of the Lok Sabha. Being second-largest gives Q no claim, seniority is irrelevant, and dissolution is not the first step after an election.

questions.stem_md: In which situation does the President have real discretion in choosing the Prime Minister?

options.text_md: When one party has won a clear majority in the Lok Sabha
When the Rajya Sabha has a different ruling party
When no party or pre-poll alliance has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha
Whenever the President disagrees with the majority party

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** When no party or pre-poll alliance has a clear majority in the Lok Sabha. If one party or alliance has a clear majority, its leader must be invited. Only in a hung House does the President judge who is most likely to win a vote of confidence. The make-up of the Rajya Sabha and personal preference play no part.

questions.stem_md: An imagined economist who is not a member of either House is sworn in as a Union minister in January. By when must she enter Parliament to keep her post?

options.text_md: Within one month
Within one year
Within six months of becoming a minister
She can never be a minister without being a member first

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Within six months of becoming a minister. A minister who is not a member of either House ceases to be a minister after 6 consecutive months unless elected or nominated in that time (Article 75(5)). So she must become a member by July. The other periods are not in the Constitution.

questions.stem_md: The Lok Sabha has 543 members. What is the largest Council of Ministers, counting the Prime Minister, that the Constitution now allows?
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 81. The 91st Amendment (2003) limits the total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, to 15 per cent of the strength of the Lok Sabha. 15 per cent of 543 is 81.45, so at most 81 ministers. The distractors use 10 per cent, a round figure and 30 per cent.

questions.stem_md: For how long does the Union Council of Ministers stay in office in practice?

options.text_md: For a fixed term of six years
Until the President completes his own term
As long as it has a majority in the Rajya Sabha
As long as it keeps the confidence of the Lok Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** As long as it keeps the confidence of the Lok Sabha. Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President, but since the President acts on ministerial advice, this means in practice for as long as the Lok Sabha supports the government. There is no fixed term, and the Rajya Sabha cannot remove it.

questions.stem_md: Before taking up office, a Union minister takes the oaths of office and secrecy. Who administers them?

options.text_md: The Prime Minister
The President
The Speaker
The Attorney General

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The President. The President administers the oaths of office and secrecy to the Prime Minister and the other ministers. The Prime Minister, Speaker and Attorney General do not.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A member of the Rajya Sabha can be appointed Prime Minister, provided the Lok Sabha supports the government.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The Constitution only requires the Prime Minister to be a member of either House (or to become one within six months). What matters is the confidence of the Lok Sabha, not the House the Prime Minister sits in.

questions.stem_md: The limit of 15 per cent of the Lok Sabha strength on the size of the Council of Ministers was added by the ___ Amendment in 2003.
questions.solution_md: The 91st Amendment (2003) added the 15 per cent ceiling and also tightened the Anti-Defection Law.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the President decides whom to appoint as Prime Minister after a general election.
questions.solution_md: Majority leader; discretion in a hung House.

answer.model_answer_md: The President invites the **leader of the party or alliance with a majority** in the **Lok Sabha**. If no group has a majority, the President uses **discretion** to invite the leader most likely to **win a vote of confidence**, who may be asked to prove it.

marking_scheme.step: Leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha
Discretion in a hung House, with a confidence vote

questions.stem_md: Why do you think the Constitution was amended to put a ceiling on the number of ministers? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Any two reasoned points: cost, rewards, defection, efficiency.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) Very large ministries had been used to **reward supporters** and keep coalitions together, which was **costly**. (2) A ceiling of **15 per cent of the Lok Sabha** keeps the government **compact** and makes posts less of a **bait for defection**.

questions.stem_md: Ministers hold office "during the pleasure of the President". Explain what this means in practice.
questions.solution_md: Formal pleasure versus practical control by the Prime Minister and the Lok Sabha.

answer.model_answer_md: Formally the President can dismiss a minister, but the President acts on the **advice of the Prime Minister**. So a minister stays as long as the **Prime Minister** wants, and the whole ministry stays as long as it has the **confidence of the Lok Sabha**.

marking_scheme.step: Acts on the Prime Minister's advice
Ministry lasts while it keeps the Lok Sabha's confidence

questions.stem_md: Which three ranks of ministers make up the Union Council of Ministers?

options.text_md: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers
Cabinet Ministers, Governors and Lieutenant Governors
Ministers of State, Secretaries and Joint Secretaries
Cabinet Ministers, judges and Election Commissioners

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers. The Council of Ministers has three ranks: Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers. Governors, civil servants such as Secretaries, judges and Election Commissioners are not ministers.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes the relationship between the Cabinet and the Council of Ministers?

options.text_md: The Cabinet is larger than the Council of Ministers
The Cabinet is a smaller inner group of senior ministers within the larger Council of Ministers
The Cabinet and the Council of Ministers are two names for exactly the same body
The Cabinet is a committee of the Rajya Sabha

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The Cabinet is a smaller inner group of senior ministers within the larger Council of Ministers. The Cabinet is the inner core: only the Cabinet Ministers. The Council of Ministers is larger and includes Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers as well. The Cabinet is part of the executive, not a committee of Parliament.

questions.stem_md: The diagram shows the ranks of the Union Council of Ministers. Which rank in it attends Cabinet meetings only when specially invited for a matter of its department?

options.text_md: Cabinet Ministers
The Prime Minister
Ministers of State
None of them ever attends

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Ministers of State. Ministers of State (in the middle tier) may hold independent charge of a department but attend Cabinet meetings only when invited. Cabinet Ministers attend as members, and the Prime Minister presides.

questions.stem_md: What is the usual role of a Deputy Minister in the Union government?

options.text_md: To preside over meetings of the Cabinet
To act as the head of the State when the President is abroad
To certify money bills
To assist a Cabinet Minister or Minister of State in the work of a department

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To assist a Cabinet Minister or Minister of State in the work of a department. Deputy Ministers have no independent charge; they help senior ministers with parliamentary and departmental work. The Prime Minister presides over the Cabinet, the Vice-President acts for the President, and the Speaker certifies money bills.

questions.stem_md: Why does the full Council of Ministers rarely meet as a body, while the Cabinet meets regularly?

options.text_md: The Constitution forbids the Council of Ministers from meeting
Only the Rajya Sabha can call the Council of Ministers together
Ministers of State are not allowed to know about government policy
The Council is too large for regular discussion, so the smaller Cabinet takes the main decisions

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Council is too large for regular discussion, so the smaller Cabinet takes the main decisions. A body of several dozen members is too big for detailed policy discussion, so decisions are taken in the Cabinet and its committees, and the Council follows them. Nothing in the Constitution forbids the Council from meeting, and the other options are false.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined minister in the Union government with the rank that fits the description.

options.text_md: Heads the Ministry of Defence and attends every Cabinet meeting
Holds independent charge of a small ministry and attends the Cabinet when invited
Helps a senior minister answer questions in the Lok Sabha; no charge of his own
Presides over the Cabinet and allocates portfolios

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Department heads in the Cabinet are Cabinet Ministers; independent charge with invitation-only attendance marks a Minister of State; assisting without charge marks a Deputy Minister; presiding and allocating portfolios is the Prime Minister's role.

questions.stem_md: Give two points of difference between the Council of Ministers and the Cabinet.
questions.solution_md: Any two: size, composition, meetings, decision-making.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Size:** the Council is **large** (all three ranks); the Cabinet is a **small** group of senior ministers. (2) **Role:** the **Cabinet takes policy decisions**; the Council as a whole **rarely meets** and carries out those decisions.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Minister of State holds independent charge of the Ministry of Tourism. Explain what "independent charge" means and whether she is a member of the Cabinet.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of independent charge; not a Cabinet member.

answer.model_answer_md: She **heads the ministry herself**, without a Cabinet Minister above her. She is **not a member of the Cabinet**; she attends Cabinet meetings **only when invited** for matters of her ministry.

marking_scheme.step: Heads the ministry without a senior minister
Not in the Cabinet; attends when invited

questions.stem_md: The Cabinet is sometimes called the real centre of power in the Union government. Give three points comparing it with the Council of Ministers that support this view.
questions.solution_md: Size, policy role, emergency advice (or another valid point).

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The Cabinet is a **small body of senior ministers**, while the Council includes many junior ministers. (2) The **Cabinet decides policy**; the Council **does not meet as a body** and carries out its decisions. (3) Advice for a **national emergency** must come from the **Cabinet** in writing, not from the whole Council.

marking_scheme.step: Emergency advice or another valid point

questions.stem_md: The Cabinet of an imagined year decides to raise farmers' crop-insurance cover and asks ministries to plan how. Which function of the Cabinet does this show most directly?

options.text_md: Judicial review
Electing the President
Policy making
Certifying a money bill

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Policy making. Deciding what the government will do in an area, here crop insurance, is policy making. Judicial review belongs to courts, the Electoral College elects the President, and the Speaker certifies money bills.

questions.stem_md: When two ministries disagree over who should build a new rail-cum-road bridge, the matter is settled in a Cabinet meeting. Which Cabinet function is this?

options.text_md: Making financial grants to States without Parliament
Coordinating the work of different departments
Amending the Constitution
Appointing judges on its own

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Coordinating the work of different departments. Resolving disputes between ministries is part of the Cabinet's administrative function of coordination. It cannot spend without Parliament, amend the Constitution alone, or appoint judges by itself.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a legislative function of the Cabinet?

options.text_md: Deciding which government bills will be introduced in Parliament and steering them through
Deciding cases between the Union and a State
Electing the Vice-President
Holding the general elections

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Deciding which government bills will be introduced in Parliament and steering them through. Most bills are government bills: the Cabinet decides on them, drafts them through ministries and guides them through Parliament. Union–State disputes go to the Supreme Court; Parliament elects the Vice-President; the Election Commission conducts elections.

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly describes the financial role of the Cabinet?

options.text_md: It can collect any tax without the approval of Parliament
It decides the budget proposals, which the Finance Minister presents to Parliament
It passes the budget without a vote of the Lok Sabha
It has no say in money matters

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** It decides the budget proposals, which the Finance Minister presents to Parliament. The Cabinet shapes the budget and the Finance Minister presents it, but no tax can be levied and no money spent without Parliament's approval. So the first option is right.

questions.stem_md: Since the 44th Amendment (1978), what must happen before the President can proclaim a national emergency?

options.text_md: The Chief Justice must approve it in writing
Half the State legislatures must ask for it
The Prime Minister alone may advise it orally
The Cabinet must recommend it to the President in writing

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The Cabinet must recommend it to the President in writing. The 44th Amendment requires a written decision of the Union Cabinet before a national emergency can be proclaimed (Article 352(3)). This was meant to prevent the Prime Minister alone from advising it. Courts and State legislatures have no such role.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because it controls the government, the Cabinet can impose a new tax by its own order without a law passed by Parliament.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** No tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law. The Cabinet proposes taxes, but Parliament must pass them.

questions.stem_md: Arrange the stages through which an imagined Cabinet proposal for a new water-saving law becomes law, in the correct order.

options.text_md: The President gives assent
The ministry concerned prepares a note and the Cabinet approves the proposal
Both Houses pass the bill
The bill is introduced in Parliament by the minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Cabinet approval comes first, then introduction by the minister, then passage in both Houses, and finally the President's assent.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: State any two administrative functions of the Union Cabinet.
questions.solution_md: Any two administrative functions.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) It **coordinates** the work of the different **ministries** and settles disputes between them. (2) It **supervises** how the laws and policies are **carried out** by the departments.

questions.stem_md: Explain why the requirement of the Cabinet's written advice for a national emergency is considered a safeguard.
questions.solution_md: Power of an emergency; collective, written decision as a check.

answer.model_answer_md: A national emergency gives the Union **great power** over the States and can affect **rights**. Requiring a **written Cabinet decision** means the **whole Cabinet** shares responsibility, so the **Prime Minister alone** cannot advise it.

marking_scheme.step: Why an emergency needs a check
Written Cabinet decision prevents one-person advice

questions.stem_md: Explain the legislative, financial and policy-making functions of the Union Cabinet, one point each.
questions.solution_md: One accurate point per function.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Legislative:** the Cabinet decides which **bills** to introduce and guides them through **Parliament**. (2) **Financial:** it prepares the **budget**, which the **Finance Minister** presents; taxes still need Parliament's approval. (3) **Policy making:** it decides the **internal and foreign policies** of the government.

questions.stem_md: To which body is the Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible under Article 75(3)?

options.text_md: The Lok Sabha
The Rajya Sabha
The Supreme Court
The President alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Lok Sabha. The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of the People, the Lok Sabha. The Rajya Sabha can question ministers but cannot remove the government; courts and the President do not hold it collectively responsible.

questions.stem_md: Individual responsibility of a Union minister means that the minister is answerable mainly to whom for the working of his department?

options.text_md: The Chief Justice of India
The State Governor
The President, acting on the Prime Minister's advice
The Comptroller and Auditor General alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The President, acting on the Prime Minister's advice. A minister holds office during the pleasure of the President; in practice the Prime Minister can ask the President to dismiss a minister whose department fails. Courts, Governors and the auditor do not remove ministers.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Cabinet Minister strongly disagrees with a Cabinet decision to sell a public company and wants to criticise it in public. What does collective responsibility require of him?

options.text_md: He may criticise it in public and stay a minister
He must ask the Supreme Court to cancel the decision
He must support the decision in public or resign from the ministry
He must ask the Rajya Sabha to overrule the Cabinet

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He must support the decision in public or resign from the ministry. Ministers may argue inside the Cabinet, but once a decision is taken they must defend it together; a minister who cannot do so should resign. Courts and the Rajya Sabha do not overrule Cabinet decisions in this way.

questions.stem_md: A serious failure is found in an imagined minister's department, and the Prime Minister asks him to quit. Which principle explains why only he leaves while the government continues?

options.text_md: Individual responsibility
Collective responsibility
Judicial review
Separation of powers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Individual responsibility. The failure is his department's, so he answers for it personally: individual responsibility. Collective responsibility would remove the whole ministry, which happens only when the Lok Sabha withdraws its confidence.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** When the Lok Sabha rejects the government's budget, all the ministers resign together.

**Reason (R):** The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Both are true. Defeat on the budget is treated as loss of confidence, and because responsibility is collective, the whole ministry resigns; R explains A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The Rajya Sabha can remove the Council of Ministers by passing a no-confidence motion.

**Reason (R):** Ministers can be asked questions in both Houses of Parliament.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A is false: only the Lok Sabha can bring down the government; a no-confidence motion cannot be moved in the Rajya Sabha. R is true: ministers answer questions in both Houses.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Ministers take an oath of secrecy before entering office.

**Reason (R):** The Prime Minister allocates portfolios among the ministers.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: (A) is true and (R) is false.
(A) is false and (R) is true.
Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Both are true, but allocating portfolios has nothing to do with the oath of secrecy, which protects confidential Cabinet discussions. So R does not explain A.

questions.stem_md: True or false? The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to both Houses of Parliament equally.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Collective responsibility is to the Lok Sabha only. The Rajya Sabha can question and criticise ministers but cannot remove the government.

questions.stem_md: Collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha is laid down in Article ___ of the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: Article 75(3) says the Council of Ministers shall be collectively responsible to the House of the People.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by collective responsibility? State one consequence of it.
questions.solution_md: Meaning plus one consequence.

answer.model_answer_md: All ministers are **jointly answerable** to the **Lok Sabha** for every decision of the government; they "**sink or swim together**". **Consequence:** if the Lok Sabha passes a **no-confidence motion**, the **whole ministry resigns**.

questions.stem_md: Explain individual responsibility of ministers with one imagined example.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and an example.

answer.model_answer_md: Each minister answers **personally** for the work of his own **department** and holds office at the **pleasure of the President**, so the **Prime Minister** can have him removed. For example, if an imagined railway minister's department fails badly, he alone may be asked to **resign**.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate why collective responsibility is important in a parliamentary democracy. Give three points.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct points on accountability, unity and shared blame.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) It keeps the government **answerable to the elected Lok Sabha**, so it cannot ignore the people's representatives. (2) It makes the ministry **speak with one voice**, giving **stable and clear** policies. (3) It forces ministers to **settle differences in private** and to **share the blame** for failures.

questions.stem_md: Why is the Prime Minister described as the real head of the executive while the President is the nominal head?

options.text_md: The Prime Minister is elected directly by all citizens
The President has no constitutional powers at all
The Prime Minister can dismiss the President at will
The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister. Article 74 makes the President act on the advice of the Council of Ministers led by the Prime Minister, so real power lies with the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister is not directly elected by all citizens, the President does have powers, and only impeachment can remove a President.

questions.stem_md: Under Article 78, which duty does the Prime Minister have towards the President?

options.text_md: To get every bill approved by the President before it goes to Parliament
To communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers about administration and proposed laws
To report only financial matters, once a year
To ask the President to preside over Cabinet meetings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** To communicate all decisions of the Council of Ministers about administration and proposed laws. The Prime Minister must keep the President informed of decisions about the administration of the Union and proposals for legislation, and give information the President asks for. The President does not pre-approve all bills or preside over the Cabinet.

questions.stem_md: After an imagined Cabinet reshuffle, the Minister of Education is moved to the Ministry of Health. Who decides such changes?

options.text_md: The Prime Minister
The Speaker
The Rajya Sabha
The Cabinet Secretary acting alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The Prime Minister. Allocating and changing portfolios is the Prime Minister's power (formally on the President's order). The Speaker, the Rajya Sabha and civil servants have no such power.

questions.stem_md: What happens to the Council of Ministers when the Prime Minister resigns?

options.text_md: Only the Prime Minister leaves; the other ministers continue as before
The whole Council of Ministers is dissolved
The senior-most Cabinet Minister automatically becomes Prime Minister for the full term
The President takes over as head of government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The whole Council of Ministers is dissolved. The Prime Minister is the head of the Council; when the Prime Minister resigns or dies, the Council of Ministers comes to an end, and a new Prime Minister forms a new ministry. There is no automatic successor for the full term, and the President does not become head of government.

questions.stem_md: An imagined Prime Minister who leads a majority wants an early general election. What step can she take?

options.text_md: Dissolve the Lok Sabha herself without informing the President
Ask the Rajya Sabha to dissolve the Lok Sabha
Advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha before its term ends
Ask the Supreme Court to call an election

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Advise the President to dissolve the Lok Sabha before its term ends. The President dissolves the Lok Sabha, normally on the advice of a Prime Minister who has the confidence of the House. The Prime Minister cannot dissolve it alone, and neither the Rajya Sabha nor the courts can.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following describes the Prime Minister's role in relation to Parliament?

options.text_md: Presiding officer of the Lok Sabha
Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
A neutral umpire who does not take sides in debates
Leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha and chief spokesperson of the government

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha and chief spokesperson of the government. The Prime Minister leads the majority, speaks for the government and defends its policies. The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha, the Vice-President chairs the Rajya Sabha, and the presiding officers, not the Prime Minister, must be neutral.

questions.stem_md: During an imagined cyclone that hits three coastal States, the Prime Minister chairs meetings of ministers, armed forces chiefs and State officials. Which role of the Prime Minister does this show?

options.text_md: Head of the State
Commander of the judiciary

questions.stem_md: True or false? The resignation or death of the Prime Minister ends the life of the whole Council of Ministers.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The Council exists around the Prime Minister as its head, so it ends when the Prime Minister leaves office; a new ministry is then formed.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the Prime Minister acts as a link between the President and the Council of Ministers.
questions.solution_md: Duty to inform; channel both ways.

answer.model_answer_md: The Prime Minister **informs the President** of all decisions of the Council about **administration and proposed laws**, and supplies information the President asks for (Article 78). The President's views reach the **Cabinet** through the Prime Minister.

questions.stem_md: State two powers of the Prime Minister in relation to the Council of Ministers.
questions.solution_md: Any two powers over the Council.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The Prime Minister advises the President on **appointing and dismissing ministers** and **allocates portfolios**. (2) The Prime Minister **presides over Cabinet meetings** and **coordinates** the work of all ministries.

questions.stem_md: An imagined new Prime Minister wants Parliament to pass her government's programme. Give two ways her position in Parliament helps her.
questions.solution_md: Two ways linked to her role in Parliament.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) As **leader of the majority** in the Lok Sabha, she can count on its **votes** for government bills. (2) As the government's **chief spokesperson**, she can **defend policies in debates** and advise on **summoning and proroguing** sessions.

questions.stem_md: The real power of a Prime Minister depends on political conditions. Explain this with two conditions.
questions.solution_md: Two conditions with their effect.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) A Prime Minister whose party has a **clear majority** usually has **more freedom** in choosing ministers and policies. (2) In a **coalition**, partners must be **consulted and kept together**, which **limits** the Prime Minister's freedom.

questions.stem_md: Give three reasons why the Prime Minister is called the head of the government and the key figure of the Union executive.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) The **President acts on the advice** of the Council of Ministers that the Prime Minister **heads**. (2) The Prime Minister **chooses ministers, allocates portfolios** and can have a minister **dismissed**. (3) The Prime Minister **leads the majority** in the Lok Sabha and **speaks for the nation** at home and abroad.

marking_scheme.step: Leader of the House and the nation

questions.stem_md:
After an imagined general election, no party wins a majority in the Lok Sabha of 543 members, but two parties form an alliance with 309 seats.

(i) Explain how the President will choose the Prime Minister in this situation. **[3]**
(ii) How are the other ministers appointed, and what limits the size of the ministry? **[3]**
(iii) Distinguish between the Council of Ministers and the Cabinet that will be formed, giving four points. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Discretion in a hung House; appointment and the ceiling; four differences.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) With no single majority, the President uses **discretion** and invites the **leader of the alliance** (309 seats, more than the 272 needed), as that leader is most likely to **command the confidence** of the Lok Sabha; the President may ask for a **vote of confidence** within a time.

(ii) The President appoints the other ministers **on the Prime Minister's advice**. A non-member may be a minister for **six months**. The total, **including the Prime Minister**, cannot exceed **15 per cent** of the Lok Sabha strength (**81** here), under the **91st Amendment (2003)**.

(iii) (1) The Council has **three ranks**; the Cabinet only **senior Cabinet Ministers**. (2) The Council is **large**; the Cabinet **small**. (3) The **Cabinet decides policy**; the Council **carries it out**. (4) The Council **rarely meets as a body**; the **Cabinet meets regularly** under the Prime Minister.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Appointed on the Prime Minister's advice; six-month rule

questions.stem_md:
The Cabinet is often described as the steering wheel of the government.

(i) Explain the policy-making and administrative functions of the Cabinet. **[3]**
(ii) Explain its legislative and financial functions. **[3]**
(iii) What is the role of the Cabinet in a national emergency? Why was this role made stricter by the 44th Amendment? **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Four functions; emergency role and the reason for the 1978 safeguard.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Policy making:** the Cabinet decides the government's **domestic and foreign policies** on matters such as farming, industry and defence. **Administrative:** it **coordinates** the ministries, **settles disputes** between them and **supervises** how policies are carried out.

(ii) **Legislative:** it decides which **bills** to introduce, and ministers **pilot them** through Parliament; it advises on **summoning and proroguing** sessions. **Financial:** it prepares the **budget** and tax proposals, presented by the **Finance Minister**; Parliament must approve them.

(iii) A **national emergency** can be proclaimed only on the **written recommendation of the Union Cabinet** (Article 352(3)). The **44th Amendment (1978)** added this so that the **Prime Minister alone** cannot advise an emergency; the **whole Cabinet** must decide and share responsibility, which protects **federalism and rights**.

questions.stem_md:
Ministers in India are answerable in two different ways.

(i) What is meant by collective responsibility? To which House does it apply, and under which Article? **[3]**
(ii) Explain individual responsibility of ministers. **[3]**
(iii) An imagined minister disagrees with a Cabinet decision, while another minister's department is found to have failed. Explain what each principle requires in these two cases. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning and Article; individual responsibility; application to two cases.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) All ministers are **jointly responsible** for every decision of the government and **stand or fall together**. It applies to the **Lok Sabha** under **Article 75(3)**; if the Lok Sabha passes a **no-confidence motion** or defeats the budget, the **whole ministry resigns**.

(ii) Each minister answers **personally** for his **department**. Ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President**, so on the **Prime Minister's advice** a minister can be **dismissed** for poor work or misconduct without the government falling.

(iii) **Disagreeing minister:** under **collective responsibility** he may argue **inside the Cabinet**, but once the decision is taken he must **defend it in public** or **resign**. **Failing department:** under **individual responsibility**, that minister may be **asked to resign** or be dismissed, while the **rest of the government continues**.

questions.stem_md:
The Prime Minister holds the central place in the Union government.

(i) Describe the powers of the Prime Minister in relation to the Council of Ministers. **[3]**
(ii) Describe the Prime Minister's role in relation to the President. **[3]**
(iii) Describe the Prime Minister's role in relation to Parliament and the nation. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Powers over the Council, the President and Parliament and nation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Prime Minister advises the President on **appointing ministers**, **allocates and changes portfolios**, can ask a minister to **resign** or have him **dismissed**, **presides over the Cabinet** and **coordinates** all ministries. If the Prime Minister resigns, the **whole Council ends**.

(ii) The Prime Minister is the **link** between the President and the Cabinet: he must **communicate all decisions** on administration and legislation (**Article 78**) and give information asked for. He **advises** the President on key **appointments** and on **dissolving** the Lok Sabha.

(iii) The Prime Minister is the **leader of the majority** in the Lok Sabha, the government's **chief spokesperson** in debates, and advises on **summoning and proroguing** Parliament. He represents the country at **international meetings** and acts as **crisis manager** in emergencies such as disasters or war.

questions.stem_md:
The President is the head of the State, but the Prime Minister is the head of the government.

(i) Why is the President called the nominal executive and the Prime Minister the real executive? **[3]**
(ii) How did the 42nd and 44th Amendments settle the question of ministerial advice to the President? **[3]**
(iii) Evaluate how the strength of a Prime Minister changes between single-party majority and coalition governments, giving two points for each. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Nominal versus real; the two amendments; a balanced evaluation.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) All executive action is taken **in the President's name**, but under **Article 74** the President acts on the **advice of the Council of Ministers** headed by the Prime Minister. So **real power** lies with the Prime Minister and the Cabinet, who are **answerable to the Lok Sabha**.

(ii) The **42nd Amendment (1976)** made the advice **binding** on the President. The **44th Amendment (1978)** let the President **return the advice once** for reconsideration, but the President must **act on the advice** given after that.

(iii) **Single-party majority:** the Prime Minister can **choose ministers freely** and push the **party's programme** without bargaining. **Coalition:** the Prime Minister must **share posts** with partners and **consult them** on policy, so decisions may be **slower** and depend on keeping the **alliance together**. In both, the Prime Minister stays the **leader**, but freedom is greater with a single majority.

marking_scheme.step: (i) Real power answerable to the Lok Sabha

questions.stem_md:
Answer the following about the term and size of the Union ministry.

(i) For how long does the Council of Ministers hold office? Explain the phrase "during the pleasure of the President". **[3]**
(ii) A person who is not a member of Parliament is made a minister. State the rule that applies and its purpose. **[3]**
(iii) With the Lok Sabha at its present membership, calculate the largest ministry allowed and explain two reasons for this limit. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Tenure in practice; six-month rule; computed ceiling and reasons.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The ministry has **no fixed term**. Ministers hold office **during the pleasure of the President**, but since the President acts on **ministerial advice**, the ministry in practice lasts as long as it keeps the **confidence of the Lok Sabha**; a minister lasts as long as the **Prime Minister** wishes.

(ii) Such a person must become a **member of either House within six months**, or cease to be a minister (Article 75(5)). This lets the government use **talented people** while keeping every minister **answerable to Parliament**.

(iii) The limit is **15 per cent** of the Lok Sabha strength, including the Prime Minister: 15 per cent of 543 is 81.45, so at most **81** ministers. **Reasons:** to cut the **cost** of oversized ministries, and to stop posts being used as **rewards for defection** in coalitions (**91st Amendment, 2003**).

marking_scheme.step: (i) No fixed term; confidence of the Lok Sabha

questions.stem_md:
Some people describe the Prime Minister as "first among equals" in the Cabinet, while others say the Prime Minister is far more than that.

(i) What does the phrase "first among equals" suggest about the Prime Minister's position? **[3]**
(ii) Give three powers that make the Prime Minister more than just one minister among others. **[3]**
(iii) Give two ways in which the Cabinet and the Lok Sabha can still check the Prime Minister, and draw a conclusion. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Meaning of the phrase; three powers; two checks and a balanced conclusion.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) It suggests that the Prime Minister is only the **senior member** of a **team of equals**, who **leads discussion** but takes decisions **together** with colleagues, in keeping with **collective responsibility**.

(ii) (1) The Prime Minister decides **who becomes a minister** and can have any minister **removed**. (2) The Prime Minister **allocates portfolios** and **presides** over the Cabinet. (3) The Prime Minister's **resignation ends the whole Council**, and only the Prime Minister can **advise dissolution** of the Lok Sabha.

(iii) (1) Senior Cabinet colleagues and **coalition partners** can **resist** decisions and even withdraw support. (2) The **Lok Sabha** can remove the government by a **no-confidence motion**. **Conclusion:** the Prime Minister is much more than first among equals, but power depends on keeping the **support** of the party and the House.

questions.stem_md:
An imagined government loses an important vote in the Lok Sabha.

(i) Explain why losing the confidence of the Lok Sabha forces the whole ministry to leave office. **[3]**
(ii) Why can the Rajya Sabha not bring down the government in the same way? **[3]**
(iii) What choices does the President have once the ministry resigns? Explain two. **[4]**
questions.solution_md: Collective responsibility; why the Rajya Sabha cannot; the President's choices.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) The Council of Ministers is **collectively responsible** to the **Lok Sabha** (**Article 75(3)**). Losing a **no-confidence motion** or a **money vote** shows it no longer has the House's **support**, so the **whole ministry** must **resign**.

(ii) The Rajya Sabha is **indirectly elected** and the ministry is **not responsible** to it. A **no-confidence motion** can be moved **only in the Lok Sabha**, and the Rajya Sabha can only **delay** money bills for **14 days**.

(iii) (1) The President may invite **another leader** who can show majority support to **form a new government**. (2) If no stable majority is possible, the President may **dissolve the Lok Sabha** on advice and order **fresh elections**, with the outgoing ministry as a **caretaker** meanwhile.

marking_scheme.step: (ii) Not responsible to the Rajya Sabha
(ii) No-confidence only in the Lok Sabha; money bills

**(b)** Not a Cabinet member; invited for her item.

**(c) (i)** Name the principle and what it requires.

**OR (c) (ii)** Size and role of the Cabinet.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** **Cabinet Ministers**, **Ministers of State** and **Deputy Ministers**.

**Diary of a new Minister of State (imagined)**

Sworn in at the President's house this morning, along with five Cabinet Ministers and three Deputy Ministers. I took two oaths, one of office and one of secrecy. I have independent charge of the Ministry of Skill Training, so no Cabinet Minister sits above me.

The Cabinet met today to decide the new apprenticeship policy. I was not in the room; I was invited only for the item on my ministry. In the meeting I argued for a larger stipend for apprentices, but the Cabinet chose a smaller one.

A reporter asked me tonight whether I would criticise the decision. I told him the government has one voice.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Draft bill for Parliament.

**(b)** Settling a dispute between ministries.

answer.model_answer_md:
